readings.title: Ivanhoe: The Palmer and the Lady Rowena (Chapter VI, part 1)
readings.challenge: Notice what the Palmer refuses and what he accepts, and listen for what his answers leave out.
readings.focus: A conversation in which both speakers hide their feelings.
readings.context: Ivanhoe (1820), by the Scottish novelist Sir Walter Scott (1771–1832), is a historical romance set in England in 1194, when King Richard the Lion-Heart, coming home from the Crusade, has been held prisoner abroad and his brother Prince John hopes to keep his throne; Saxon families such as Cedric’s still resent the Norman lords who conquered England in 1066. This chapter is headed “CHAPTER VII.” in the first edition, which repeats that number; later editions call it Chapter VI. A stranger dressed as a Palmer, a pilgrim back from the Holy Land, is spending the night at Rotherwood, the hall of the Saxon Cedric, where at supper he defended the absent Knight of Ivanhoe against the Templar Brian de Bois-Guilbert. Cedric has disowned his son Wilfred of Ivanhoe, and plans to marry his ward, the Lady Rowena, to the Saxon prince Athelstane. The motto comes from Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice. Mead is a drink made from honey; curfew was the evening bell; a solere is an upper chamber; benison is blessing; a genuflection is a bow on one knee; a pennon is a small flag; a tourney is a tournament; Cœur-de-Lion is King Richard.
readings.contentNote: This historical novel imagines twelfth-century England through nineteenth-century assumptions. Its national, religious, racial and class generalizations are perspectives to examine, not reliable descriptions of whole peoples. Historical insults appear in the original text.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the sixth chapter (printed “CHAPTER VII.”), from its motto to the Palmer’s leaving Rowena’s room; opens “To buy his favour I extend this friendship: If he will take it, so; if not, adieu; And,…”; closes “…accepted the boon with another low reverence, and followed Edwina out of the apartment.”.

questions.prompt: The Palmer refuses the servants’ invitation to drink and talk, but obeys Rowena’s summons. What reason does he give for refusing, and what might his real reasons be?
facilitatorNotes: He claims a vow never to speak in the kitchen of matters forbidden in the hall: Cedric has banned talk of Ivanhoe, and he will not gossip behind his host’s back. Yet he follows Rowena’s maid “without answer or remonstrance.” Readers may suspect a personal interest in Rowena; the offended cup-bearer lodges him next to Isaac as a punishment.
evidence: an obligation never to speak in the kitchen on matters which were prohibited in the hall
he obeyed it without answer or remonstrance

questions.prompt: How does Scott describe Rowena’s room? What is the point of “let not modern beauty envy the magnificence of a Saxon princess”?
facilitatorNotes: Silk hangings worked with gold and silver, purple curtains, an ivory footstool, four silver candelabra; but the walls are so full of cracks that the hangings shake and the flames blow sideways. There is magnificence without comfort, and “being unknown, it was unmissed.” Scott speaks directly to his 1820 readers, warning them not to romanticise the past.
evidence: Yet let not modern beauty envy the magnificence of a Saxon princess.
but of comfort there was little, and, being unknown, it was unmissed

questions.prompt: Rowena finds it hard to say the name “Ivanhoe.” What shows her feelings, and why must she ask a stranger about him?
facilitatorNotes: She pauses, speaks “with a sort of effort,” sighs, and asks whether illness has spoiled his strength and looks. In Cedric’s hall the name is banned, so of all those who care for him she alone dares to ask. She also fears what he will find if Athelstane wins the tournament.
evidence: the name of Ivanhoe, in the halls where by nature and kindred it should have sounded most acceptably
Had disease laid her hand heavy upon his strength and comeliness?

questions.prompt: The Palmer answers “with a troubled voice” and says he hardly knows Ivanhoe. What clues suggest he knows more than he says?
facilitatorNotes: He wishes he knew Ivanhoe better “since you, lady, are interested in his fate”; yet he knows his route home, his command of French, and that he was “darker … and thinner” than when he came from Cyprus, while claiming never to have approached him. Readers may begin to guess who the Palmer is; Scott lets us suspect more than Rowena does.
evidence: answered the Palmer, with a troubled voice
but I approached not his presence, because he is unknown to me

readings.title: Ivanhoe: A Warning before Dawn (Chapter VI, part 2)
readings.challenge: Compare what the Palmer says about Isaac with how he treats him, and follow Isaac from terror to suspicion to hope.
readings.focus: A rescue offered with contempt, and a victim who has learned to distrust help.
readings.context: Recap: the Palmer, a mysterious pilgrim staying the night at Cedric’s hall of Rotherwood, has told the Lady Rowena what little he says he knows of the banished Knight of Ivanhoe. Isaac of York, a Jewish moneylender, has also been given shelter; at supper the Templar Brian de Bois-Guilbert and his Saracen (Muslim) slaves showed open hatred of him. St Dunstan was an English saint; matins are morning prayers; to be “abstracted” is to be stolen; a Musselman is a Muslim; Philip de Malvoisin and Reginald Front-de-Bœuf are Norman barons; the rack was an instrument of torture; Isaac recalls the Bible’s account of captives of Rabbah put under saws and axes; Lazarus is the beggar in Jesus’s parable; an Ishmaelite here is a Muslim; to “gird up our loins” is to make ready for a journey. The 1820 printing has no stop after “the mixed language of the country” before Isaac’s cry, nor after “his pilgrim’s staff”; the text follows the page as printed.
readings.contentNote: Servants insult Isaac in antisemitic terms, Isaac dreams of torture, and the Palmer’s help is mixed with contempt. Scott shows these prejudices to expose them, but his narration also shares some of its age’s stereotypes; they are perspectives to examine, not descriptions of a people.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the sixth chapter (printed “CHAPTER VII.”), from the cells of the household to Isaac’s decision to flee; opens “In the anti-room he found his attendant Anwold, who, taking the torch from the hand of…”; closes “…urgency of his companion; "but I must secure the means of leaving this place—follow me."”.

questions.prompt: What do Anwold’s words about Isaac show about the household? How does the Palmer answer him?
facilitatorNotes: Isaac “kennels” like a dog, and his cell will need scraping before a Christian can use it; the Palmer is lodged between the Jew and the swineherd as a slight. He replies that a Jew’s company “can hardly spread contamination through an oaken partition”: a dry rebuke, though it still plays with the idea of contamination.
evidence: kennels in the cell next your holiness
the company, even of a Jew, can hardly spread contamination through an oaken partition

questions.prompt: What is Isaac dreaming, and why does Scott show the dream before the Palmer speaks?
facilitatorNotes: He sleeps with his clothes arranged around him against theft and cries out that he is poor and that torturers’ irons could get nothing from him. The dream shows the fear of torture for money that Jews of the time lived with, and it makes the Palmer’s news a nightmare come true: “the dream is not dreamed for nought.”
evidence: should your irons wrench my limbs asunder, I could not gratify you!
the dream is not dreamed for nought

questions.prompt: What has the Palmer overheard, and how could he understand it? What does this suggest about him?
facilitatorNotes: The Templar ordered his slaves, in “the Saracen language,” to seize Isaac on the road and carry him to a Norman baron’s castle, where he could be squeezed for money. The Palmer understands that language, which suggests long years in the East and more than a simple pilgrim’s past.
evidence: in the Saracen language, which I well understand
to seize upon him when at a convenient distance from the mansion

questions.prompt: The Palmer views Isaac’s terror “with a compassion in which contempt was largely mingled,” and pulls away from his touch “as if there were contamination.” How does this fit with what he said to Anwold? What do you make of his help?
facilitatorNotes: Last night he mocked the idea of contamination; now he acts it out. He helps sincerely and admits the Jews’ persecution (“you have cause for your terror”), yet shares his age’s prejudice. Isaac, for his part, expects that help must be bought: “there is but one road to the favour of a Christian.” Readers may see Scott showing that even a good knight of 1194 is not free of prejudice, or may think the narrator half shares it.
evidence: with a compassion in which contempt was largely mingled
The Pilgrim extricated himself, as if there were contamination in the touch.
there is but one road to the favour of a Christian

readings.title: Ivanhoe: Out by the Postern (Chapter VI, part 3)
readings.challenge: Work out what a whispered word must have been from its effects, and separate Scott’s history from his generalizations.
readings.focus: Judging from appearances, and the narrator stepping outside the story.
readings.context: Recap: at dawn the Palmer has warned Isaac of York that the Templar’s Saracen slaves mean to seize him on the road and carry him to a Norman baron’s castle, to be tortured for money; terrified and suspicious, Isaac has agreed to flee with him. Gurth is Cedric’s swineherd and Wamba his jester, both born serfs. A postern is a back gate; Eumæus is the loyal swineherd of Homer’s Odyssey; a pallet is a straw bed; a gammon is a ham; anon means soon; “I trow” means I believe; a palisade is a fence of stakes and a wicket a small gate in it; buckram is stiff cloth; a gaberdine is a long loose coat; “en croupe” means behind the saddle; certes means certainly; an ambuscade is an ambush; the Jews’ Exchequer was a royal court for taxing England’s Jews; bills of exchange are written orders to pay money in another place.
readings.contentNote: In a digression Scott describes the persecution and torture of England’s medieval Jews, including King John’s having a Jew’s teeth pulled out one a day. He condemns the persecution, yet also repeats stereotypes of Jewish “avarice” and “obstinacy”; these are his generalizations, to be examined, not accepted.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the sixth chapter (printed “CHAPTER VII.”), from the waking of Gurth to the narrator’s account of the Jews of the period; opens “He led the way to the adjoining cell, which, as the reader is apprised, was occupied by…”; closes “…obstinate, uncomplying, and skilful in evading the dangers to which they were exposed.”.

questions.prompt: Gurth refuses the Palmer until he hears a whisper. What changes, and what might the Palmer have said?
facilitatorNotes: Gurth is offended by the commanding tone and insists no guest leaves by stealth. A few words in Saxon make him start “as if electrified”; he hurries to obey, fetches the mules and kisses the Palmer’s hand “with the utmost possible veneration.” The Palmer must have told him something about himself; Scott withholds the words, and readers may guess.
evidence: Gurth started up as if electrified.
who kissed it with the utmost possible veneration

questions.prompt: What does Wamba suspect, and how does Gurth’s reply, “thou arguest from appearances, and the wisest of us can do no more,” apply to the whole chapter?
facilitatorNotes: Wamba jokes that palmers must learn something “more potent” than prayer, and guesses the Palmer is a Norman. Gurth praises him for reasoning from appearances, which is all anyone can do. Everyone here judges by appearances: the servants’ contempt, Isaac’s suspicion, the Palmer’s disguise.
evidence: Something more potent than that
though thou arguest from appearances, and the wisest of us can do no more

questions.prompt: What does Isaac do with the blue bag, and how does Scott seem to want readers to take it?
facilitatorNotes: He mutters that it holds “only a change of raiment” and hides it under his coat: the reader infers money. The comedy plays on the stereotype of the secretive Jew, but the next paragraphs explain why a hunted man hides his means. Readers can discuss whether the joke is at Isaac’s expense.
evidence: a change of raiment—only a change of raiment
so disposing the skirts of his gaberdine as to conceal completely from observation the burthen

questions.prompt: In the long paragraphs on the Jews of this period, Scott steps out of the story. What does he condemn, and where does his own description fall into stereotype?
facilitatorNotes: He condemns an “unintermitting, general, and relentless persecution”: every people of England united in hating them, kings and nobles torturing them for money, a court made to plunder them. Yet he explains their survival by “the love of gain” and speaks of “the obstinacy and avarice of the Jews,” giving a whole people traits. Readers should separate his historical sympathy from his generalizations; it also explains why Isaac’s suspicion of the Palmer “might have been indeed pardoned.”
evidence: who were the object of such an unintermitting, general, and relentless persecution
The obstinacy and avarice of the Jews

readings.title: Ivanhoe: The Parting at Sheffield (Chapter VI, part 4)
readings.challenge: Track how each man reads the other, and who finally gives more.
readings.focus: Suspicion turning into a wary trust; a stereotype voiced and then overturned.
readings.context: Recap: the Palmer, a mysterious pilgrim, has led Isaac of York out of Cedric’s hall at dawn to save him from the Templar’s plan to kidnap him, and they are riding hard through the forest; Scott has paused to describe how cruelly medieval England persecuted its Jews. Pharaoh’s chariots lost their wheels in the Red Sea in Exodus; succour is help; to requite is to repay; Sheffield is a town in Yorkshire; gyves are shackles, and “in thy danger” means in debt to you; the Holy Sepulchre is the tomb of Jesus in Jerusalem; Milan harnesses are suits of armour made in Milan; the rod of Moses worked miracles; colic is a painful stomach cramp; “usage money” is interest; a hurley-burley is an uproar; gramercy means thank you.
readings.contentNote: The Palmer repeats the stereotype that Jews “give nothing for nothing,” and Scott plays Isaac’s struggle for comedy; Isaac’s generosity in the scene works against the stereotype.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the sixth chapter (printed “CHAPTER VII.”), from the decayed oak to the end of the chapter; opens “When the travellers had pushed on at a rapid rate through many devious paths, the Palmer…”; closes “They parted, and took different roads for the town of Sheffield.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the Palmer want to part from Isaac, and why does he agree to go as far as Sheffield? What does his reasoning show?
facilitatorNotes: It “beseems not” a pilgrim and a Jew to travel together; yet protecting a Jew against a Saracen “can scarce be accounted unworthy of a Christian.” He finds a reason in religious rank that lets him help: he protects Isaac while keeping his distance.
evidence: for it beseems not men of my character and thine to travel together
since to protect a Jew against a Saracen, can scarce be accounted unworthy of a Christian

questions.prompt: How does Isaac guess what the Palmer most wants? What has he noticed?
facilitatorNotes: Words that showed “like sparks from flint … the metal within,” and a knight’s gold chain and spurs glimpsed under the gown when the Palmer leaned over his bed. Isaac is a sharp observer. The startled Palmer answers with a joke: searching Isaac’s clothes would reveal secrets too. Each man hides a treasure.
evidence: in the bosom of that Palmer's gown, is hidden a knight's chain and spurs of gold
Were thy garments searched by as curious an eye, Isaac

questions.prompt: What does Isaac offer, and how does the Palmer test him? Who comes out better?
facilitatorNotes: A letter in Hebrew to a kinsman at Leicester who will lend the best horse and armour for the tournament. The Palmer points out that a loser’s arms are forfeit and says “those of thy tribe give nothing for nothing.” Isaac squirms comically, but “his better feelings predominated”: he waives damage and interest and worries about the young man’s life. His generosity overturns the stereotype, though Scott plays his struggle for laughs.
evidence: his better feelings predominated over those which were most familiar to him
but for the sake of thine own life and limbs

questions.prompt: Compare the Palmer’s request about Isaac’s debtors with Isaac’s last warning. What does each man think of the other at the end?
facilitatorNotes: The Palmer asks him to spare some Christian debtor “the gyves and the dungeon,” assuming Isaac is a hard creditor; Isaac’s parting words show real care for the Palmer himself. The Palmer smiles and promises to repay the courtesy. Mutual suspicion has become a wary trust; readers can judge how far the Palmer has changed.
evidence: spare the gyves and the dungeon to some unhappy Christian who stands in thy danger
Gramercy for thy caution

readings.title: Ivanhoe: England in 1194 (Chapter VII, part 1)
readings.challenge: Follow a chain of historical causes, and notice how Scott sets glamour against hardship.
readings.focus: The troubled kingdom behind the tournament, and a narrator who judges before we meet his characters.
readings.context: Ivanhoe (1820), by the Scottish novelist Sir Walter Scott (1771–1832), is a historical romance set in England in 1194, when King Richard the Lion-Heart, coming home from the Crusade, has been held prisoner abroad and his brother Prince John hopes to keep his throne; Saxon families such as Cedric’s still resent the Norman lords who conquered England in 1066. This chapter is headed “CHAPTER VIII.” in the first edition, which had numbered an earlier chapter twice; later editions call it Chapter VII. After the Palmer parted from Isaac at Sheffield, Scott turns to the great tournament at Ashby, toward which all his characters are travelling. The motto comes from John Dryden’s version of Chaucer’s Knight’s Tale, “Palamon and Arcite.” Liveries are uniforms; a buckler is a shield; a palfrey is a riding horse; “subaltern” oppression is oppression by petty officials; Arthur of Brittany, son of John’s elder brother Geoffrey, had a better claim to the throne than John; profligate means wasteful and immoral; perfidious means treacherous; the forest laws reserved hunting in royal forests for the king, with savage penalties; usurious interest is excessive interest; cankers are spreading sores; a real was a small Spanish coin, and a bull-feast is a bullfight; a Passage of Arms is a tournament in which a group of challengers holds the field against all comers.
readings.contentNote: Scott blames the nobles’ debts partly on Jewish moneylenders’ “usurious interest” and says nobles escaped their creditors by violence; this reflects the novel’s nineteenth-century assumptions about medieval Jews.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the seventh chapter (printed “CHAPTER VIII.”), from its motto to the crowds hastening to Ashby; opens “Knights, with a long retinue of their squires, In gaudy liveries march and quaint…”; closes “…of persons of all ranks hastened upon the appointed morning to the place of combat.”.

questions.prompt: Scott opens with England’s troubles. Name three, and explain how they feed one another.
facilitatorNotes: King Richard is a prisoner; John plots with Philip of France against Richard and against Arthur, gathering hardened crusaders who hope for civil war; oppression and the forest laws drive men into outlaw bands; nobles act as petty tyrants, borrow heavily and turn on their creditors; disease strikes the poor hardest. With no king to give justice, each trouble breeds the next.
evidence: King Richard was absent a prisoner
a prey to every species of subaltern oppression

questions.prompt: How does Scott describe Prince John before he even appears? What effect does this have on how we will see him?
facilitatorNotes: “Light, profligate, and perfidious,” working to keep in prison the brother to whom he owed so many favours. Telling us first makes us watch John’s actions for proof. Some readers may prefer to judge characters from what they do rather than from the narrator’s verdict.
evidence: His own character being light, profligate, and perfidious
to prolong the captivity of his brother Richard, to whom he stood indebted for so many favours

questions.prompt: Why does Scott compare the tournament crowd to “the half-starved citizen of Madrid” at a bullfight? Is the comparison fair?
facilitatorNotes: Rich and poor alike, in the middle of misery, crave a spectacle, as a starving man spends his thought on a bullfight. Scott, writing for readers of 1820, links the past with his own time; the comparison suggests escape and perhaps folly. Readers may think of the spectacles of their own day.
evidence: the half-starved citizen of Madrid, who has not a real left to buy provisions for his family
Neither duty nor infirmity could keep youth or age from such exhibitions.

questions.prompt: The motto lists knights in “gaudy liveries,” smiths, yeomen and “clowns … with cudgels.” How does it set up the chapter, compared with the history that follows?
facilitatorNotes: The motto gives chivalry’s bright, festive side: colours, gold bits, eager horses and crowds. The history gives prison, plots, outlaws and plague. Scott sets the glamour of the tournament against the misery around it, a contrast the coming scenes will play out.
evidence: In gaudy liveries march and quaint attires
The condition of the English nation was at this time sufficiently miserable.

readings.title: Ivanhoe: The Lists at Ashby (Chapter VII, part 2)
readings.challenge: Build a clear picture of a place from a long description, and notice who is placed where.
readings.focus: A stage set for conflict: space, rank and suspense.
readings.context: Recap: Scott has described England in 1194, with King Richard a prisoner, Prince John plotting to take the throne, outlaws in the forests and nobles acting as petty tyrants; yet rich and poor flock to the great tournament at Ashby. The lists are the fenced ground where knights fight on horseback; palisades are fences of stakes; heralds proclaim and judge rank, helped by pursuivants; pavilions are large tents; “sylvan” means of the woods; an esplanade is a level open space; farriers shoe horses; the pit was the floor of a theatre below the boxes; the promiscuous multitude is the mixed crowd; emblazoned means painted as on a coat of arms; La Royne de la Beaulté et des Amours is Old French for the Queen of Beauty and of Love; marshals keep order on the field; “refractory” means unruly.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the seventh chapter (printed “CHAPTER VIII.”), from “The scene was singularly romantic” to the filling of the galleries; opens “The scene was singularly romantic. On the verge of a wood, which approached to within a…”; closes “…It was of course amongst these that the most frequent disputes for precedence occurred.”.

questions.prompt: Describe, or sketch, the layout of the lists. Where are the challengers, where will other knights enter, and where will Prince John sit?
facilitatorNotes: A quarter-mile square with rounded corners in a hollow meadow; through the south gate a slope up to five black-and-russet pavilions for the challengers; at the north gate an enclosure for knights who will answer them; the Prince’s raised gallery in the middle of the east side, opposite the point of impact, and the Queen of Beauty’s gallery facing it on the west.
evidence: five magnificent pavilions, adorned with pennons of russet and black
exactly opposite to the spot where the shock of the combat must take place

questions.prompt: Who are the five challengers? Which names have you met before, and what might that suggest about the tournament?
facilitatorNotes: Brian de Bois-Guilbert, the Templar who planned to seize Isaac, has the place of honour; beside him are Reginald Front-de-Bœuf, one of the two barons to whose castles the Templar meant Isaac to be carried, and Richard de Malvoisin, who shares the other baron’s name; then Grentmesnil and Vipont. All are Normans, and several are men we have seen scheming against a defenceless guest, so readers may expect the challengers to be the villains and wonder who will answer them.
evidence: The central pavilion, as the place of honour, had been assigned to Brian de Bois-Guilbert
On one side of his tent were pitched those of Reginald Front-de-Bœuf and Richard de Malvoisin

questions.prompt: How does the seating sort the crowd by rank? Find the comparison Scott uses to make it familiar to his readers.
facilitatorNotes: Nobles and ladies sit in tapestried galleries; yeomen and better-off spectators in a narrow space “compared to the pit of a theatre”; the mixed crowd on banks of turf; others in trees and even a church steeple. Even quarrels over seats are settled by rank: axe-shafts for commoners, heralds for their betters.
evidence: might be compared to the pit of a theatre
being readily employed as arguments to convince the most refractory

questions.prompt: What does Scott find surprising about the ladies, and what mystery does he leave unsolved?
facilitatorNotes: More ladies than men come to a sport “too bloody and dangerous,” one would think, to please them. And the throne of the Queen of Beauty and of Love, hung with Cupid’s “common-place emblems,” has no named occupant. Scott’s irony touches the clichés of romance, while the empty throne creates suspense: someone will have to choose her.
evidence: a sport, which one would have thought too bloody and dangerous to afford them much pleasure
But who the Queen of Beauty and of Love was to prove, no one was prepared to guess.

readings.title: Ivanhoe: Isaac Seeks a Place, and Prince John Arrives (Chapter VII, part 3)
readings.challenge: Look behind the confidence or splendour of each figure for the calculation or character beneath it.
readings.focus: Wealth, rank and power in a crowd, and appearances the crowd mistakes for character.
readings.context: Recap: the tournament ground at Ashby is filling. Five Norman challengers, among them the Templar Bois-Guilbert, Front-de-Bœuf and Malvoisin, hold the field; galleries await Prince John and the unnamed Queen of Beauty and of Love; crowds quarrel over places. Isaac of York has come after his flight from Cedric’s hall. A gaberdine is a long coat; Montdidier is an old Norman family; Lincoln green is the cloth foresters wore; a baldric is a shoulder belt; the Prior of Jorvaulx, Prior Aymer, appeared earlier in the novel; Knights Templars and Knights of St John (Hospitallers) were orders of warrior monks; Saladin was the sultan who held Jerusalem; contemned means despised; to caracole is to prance in half-turns; a rheno is a fur cape; sables are costly furs; maroquin is fine goatskin leather.
readings.contentNote: An impoverished Norman and a yeoman insult Isaac in antisemitic terms (“Dog of an unbeliever”; “sucking the blood of his miserable victims”), and the narration presents Jews as moneylenders who survived by noble protection.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the seventh chapter (printed “CHAPTER VIII.”), from the quarrel over Isaac’s place to the crowd’s applause for Prince John; opens “"Dog of an unbeliever," said an old man, whose thread-bare tunic bore witness to his…”; closes “…with which he managed his palfrey, were sufficient to merit their clamorous applause.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Isaac, so timid at Rotherwood, now push boldly into the front row? What does Scott’s explanation tell us about his position?
facilitatorNotes: In a public place no noble dares harm him; the law and self-interested barons protect him; and Prince John is negotiating a large loan from the Jews of York in which Isaac has a big share. His boldness is a calculation: his safety depends on his usefulness to the powerful.
evidence: knew well that upon the present he had nothing to fear
Prince John was even then in the very act of negociating a large loan from the Jews of York

questions.prompt: Compare the two men who object to Isaac. What does each have, and what does each lack?
facilitatorNotes: The old Norman has rank without money: a threadbare tunic with sword, dagger and gold chain. The yeoman has skill and self-confidence: a forester’s dress, twelve arrows, a six-foot bow. Both resent Isaac’s wealth, and the yeoman’s “bottled spider” image is cruel. The bystanders side with the poor Norman.
evidence: whose thread-bare tunic bore witness to his poverty
swelled him like a bottled spider

questions.prompt: How does Scott use the Prior of Jorvaulx’s boots to comment on Prince John’s followers?
facilitatorNotes: Their points curl so far that they are tied to his belt, so he cannot use his stirrups: absurd vanity in a churchman, who perhaps enjoys showing off his riding to the ladies. Laymen and clergy in John’s train are equally “light” and “gay,” with mercenaries and marauding barons among them.
evidence: as light in their dress, and as gay in their demeanour as their companions
effectually prevented him from putting his foot into the stirrup

questions.prompt: Scott says the Prince’s open, handsome face “is often mistaken for manly frankness.” What does he say it really shows, and how does most of the crowd judge him?
facilitatorNotes: The “reckless indifference” of a pleasure-seeker sure of his superior birth. The crowd, “a hundred to one,” judges by his furs, boots, golden spurs and graceful riding, and cheers. Again appearance and character part company, and the narrator asks us to look deeper than the crowd.
evidence: Such an expression is often mistaken for manly frankness
were sufficient to merit their clamorous applause

readings.title: Ivanhoe: Rebecca, and the Saxons’ Gallery (Chapter VII, part 4)
readings.challenge: Ask whose eyes the description looks through, and what each insult is meant to achieve.
readings.focus: Mockery as a political weapon; a description that makes a woman something to be looked at.
readings.context: Recap: at the Ashby tournament Isaac of York, sure of Prince John’s protection because the Prince needs a loan, has pushed into the front row with his daughter Rebecca and been insulted by bystanders; now the handsome, contemptuous Prince rides round the lists with his frivolous followers, among them Prior Aymer of Jorvaulx. Aquiline means hooked like an eagle’s beak; a simarre is a long robe; an agraffe is a jewelled clasp; “the wisest king who ever lived” is Solomon, and the Canticles (the Song of Songs), the Bible’s love poem traditionally ascribed to him, supplies the rose of Sharon and the lily of the valley; Mammon is wealth; marks and byzants are coins; an houri is a beautiful maiden of the Muslim paradise; a congee is a bow; hinds and churls are peasants; Athelstane, here “of Conigsmark,” descends from the last Saxon kings; vis inertiæ is Latin for the force of inertia.
readings.contentNote: Prince John mocks Isaac with antisemitic insults and leers at Rebecca, and the narrator’s own description lingers on her body and her “Eastern” difference. Athelstane is said to be a heavy drinker.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the seventh chapter (printed “CHAPTER VIII.”), from the Prince’s first sight of Rebecca to Athelstane’s stare; opens “In his joyous caracole round the lists; the attention of the Prince was called by the…”; closes “…in it something extremely ludicrous. But the impatient John regarded it in no such light.”.

questions.prompt: How does Scott describe Rebecca? Which details present her as beautiful, and which as foreign? Whose eyes are we looking through?
facilitatorNotes: Her figure, dark complexion, eyes, brows, teeth and curls; her turban, “Eastern dress,” Persian silk, ostrich feather and diamonds. The narrator invokes Prince John as a “shrewd connoisseur” and dwells on her neck and unfastened clasps: a male outsider’s gaze that makes her something to be looked at. The proud ladies scoff but secretly envy. Readers can watch whether later chapters give her a voice of her own.
evidence: even though it had been judged by as shrewd a connoisseur as Prince John
scoffed and sneered at by the proud dames who sat above her, but secretly envied by those who affected to deride them

questions.prompt: Prince John calls Isaac “my prince of usurers” and orders him a seat in the gallery. Why honour him and insult him at the same time?
facilitatorNotes: Isaac is his source of money, “my prince of supplies,” and the favour costs John nothing while it shows his power. The honour is a joke at Isaac’s expense, “at least as much mockery as courtesy,” and his followers laugh obediently. Isaac answers with a bow, “nothing embarrassed.”
evidence: my prince of supplies, with his lovely Jewess, shall have a place in the gallery
in which, however, there was at least as much mockery as courtesy

questions.prompt: Why does John choose Cedric’s and Athelstane’s places in particular?
facilitatorNotes: Scott has told us John hates the few powerful Saxon families and never misses a chance to affront them. Forcing proud Saxon nobles to make room for a Jew humiliates both at once; “Saxon churls!” shows the contempt.
evidence: Saxon churls!—out upon them!
the family of Cedric the Saxon, with that of his ally and kinsman Athelstane

questions.prompt: How does Athelstane respond to the order? How do his friends and his critics explain his character, and which explanation does Scott seem to favour?
facilitatorNotes: He neither obeys nor resists; he simply stares, opposing only “the vis inertiæ,” which is “extremely ludicrous.” Friends say he lacks decision, not courage; others blame inherited drunkenness and “brutal debauchery.” Scott gives the harsher view the last and longest word. Readers may compare him with Cedric, who is about to act.
evidence: he was very generally called Athelstane the Unready
opposed only the vis inertiæ to the will of John

readings.title: Ivanhoe: A Lance, a Bow and a Shield of Brawn (Chapter VII, part 5)
readings.challenge: Follow a confrontation that turns from violence to laughter, and weigh who wins and who pays.
readings.focus: Courage, a hidden threat, a cruel joke and a theft applauded as generosity.
readings.context: Recap: at the Ashby tournament Prince John, to humiliate the Saxons, has ordered Cedric and the slow Athelstane to make room in their gallery for Isaac of York and his daughter Rebecca; Athelstane only stares. Bracy is Maurice de Bracy, leader of “free companions,” mercenaries (Condottieri) who fight for pay; a yeoman is a free commoner; to “hit the white” is to hit the centre of a target; King William Rufus was killed by an arrow, said to be Walter Tyrrell’s, while hunting in 1100 (Scott calls him John’s grandfather; he was a more distant relative); churls are peasants; “an it please” means if it please; horse-furniture is harness; brawn is boar’s meat, here a ham, which Jewish law forbids; an alderman is a town official; a jennet is a small horse; byzants are gold coins.
readings.contentNote: Prince John calls Isaac “infidel dog” and threatens to have him flayed; Wamba thrusts pork in his face and Isaac falls down the steps to the crowd’s laughter; John then takes his purse. The scene shows public cruelty to a Jew treated as entertainment.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the seventh chapter (printed “CHAPTER VIII.”), from Bracy’s lance to the end of the chapter; opens “"The Saxon porker," he said, "is either asleep or minds me not—Prick him with your lance,…”; closes “…as much applause from the spectators as if he had done some honest and honourable action.”.

questions.prompt: How do Athelstane and Cedric respond to Bracy’s lance? What does the crowd’s reaction show?
facilitatorNotes: Athelstane cannot even draw back; Cedric, “as prompt as his companion was tardy,” cuts off the lance-point with one blow. Even John’s attendants murmured at the order, and the crowd cheers Cedric: popular feeling is against the Prince, who looks round for “some safe and easy victim.”
evidence: as prompt as his companion was tardy
a general exclamation of the crowd uttered in loud applause of the spirited conduct of Cedric

questions.prompt: What is dangerous about the yeoman’s answers and the voice from the crowd? Why does John back down?
facilitatorNotes: The yeoman calmly says he cheers any good shot or blow and can hit a woodsman’s mark; an unseen voice adds “Wat Tyrrell's mark,” a reminder that a king was once killed by an arrow. The veiled threat “incensed and alarmed” John; he has the archer watched and promises to test his skill, which sets up a later trial.
evidence: I always add my hollo
This allusion to the fate of William Rufus

questions.prompt: Wamba heads off a clash between Cedric and the Prince by thrusting a ham in Isaac’s face. Why does the crowd laugh, and how should a reader respond to the joke?
facilitatorNotes: The ham is pork, forbidden to Jews; Isaac recoils, falls down the steps, and everyone, John included, laughs while Wamba claims the prize. The jest heads off a fight between Cedric and the Prince, protecting Wamba’s master, but it is paid for by the humiliation of an old man. Readers can see it as both quick-witted and cruel.
evidence: The catastrophe was prevented by the clown Wamba
an excellent jest to the spectators, who set up a loud laughter

questions.prompt: Reread the last sentence. What is Scott’s judgment of John’s “generosity,” and of the crowd?
facilitatorNotes: John asks to borrow “a handful” of coins, snatches the whole purse, tosses two pieces to Wamba and rides on, applauded “as if he had done some honest and honourable action.” The irony exposes theft dressed as generosity and a crowd that cheers splendour. Isaac’s confidence in the Prince’s protection has proved hollow.
evidence: settled Isaac's doubts by snatching the pouch itself from his side
as if he had done some honest and honourable action

readings.title: Ivanhoe: A Jest, and the Laws of the Lists (Chapter VIII, part 1)
readings.challenge: Notice who objects to Prince John’s jest and on what grounds, and keep the four laws of the tournament straight.
readings.focus: A prince whose followers must manage him, and a ceremony that turns combat into rules.
readings.context: Recap: at the tournament of Ashby, Prince John has insulted the Saxon Cedric and Isaac of York, been answered boldly by a yeoman archer, and ridden off with Isaac’s purse while the crowd laughed. This chapter is headed “CHAPTER IX.” in the first edition, which had numbered an earlier chapter twice; later editions call it Chapter VIII. The motto comes from “Palamon and Arcite,” a poem about two knights who fight for one lady. “By my halidom” is an oath (by my holy relics); the Prior of Jorvaulx is the head of an abbey; to “gage” is to pledge; a palfrey is a riding horse; the “arms of courtesy” are blunted lances; “at outrance” (French à outrance) means to the death; largesse is a shower of gifts; cap-a-pee means from head to foot; a span is about nine inches, and pennons are small flags.
readings.contentNote: Prince John proposes Rebecca, a Jewish woman, as Queen of Beauty only to insult the Saxons, lumping them together as “dog or hog,” and the Prior answers “a Jewess!” in horror. Scott presents the jest as an insult even John’s own followers reject; the scene shows the period’s contempt for Jews.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the eighth chapter (printed “CHAPTER IX.”), from its motto to the knights crowding the northern end of the lists; opens “At this the challenger with fierce defy His trumpet sounds; the challenged makes reply:…”; closes “…them, joined with the restless motion of the feathers to add liveliness to the scene.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Prince John propose Rebecca as Queen of Love and Beauty? What does “Saxon or Jew, dog or hog” show about how he sees both?
facilitatorNotes: Not from admiration: he wants “to mortify the Saxon churls.” His phrase lumps Saxons and Jews with animals; Rebecca is only a tool for an insult. The Prior’s horror shows a different prejudice, the fear of scandal (“stoned out of the lists”).
evidence: were it only to mortify the Saxon churls
Saxon or Jew, dog or hog, what matters it?

questions.prompt: Bracy and Waldemar Fitzurse both object. What reason does each give, and what does John’s retreat (“I did but jest”) show about who holds power?
facilitatorNotes: Bracy says no knight would fight under such an insult; Waldemar says it would ruin John’s plans and claims a counsellor’s right, since his own safety is staked with John’s. John gives way at Waldemar’s tone: he depends on followers he cannot afford to lose. Students may notice that the objection is to insulting the knights, not to using Rebecca.
evidence: no knight here will lay lance in rest if such an insult is attempted
your interest and safety are not more deeply gaged than theirs
I did but jest

questions.prompt: What is the difference between touching a challenger’s shield with the reverse of the lance and with the sharp end? Why does Scott spell out the rules before any fighting?
facilitatorNotes: The reverse chooses the arms of courtesy, lances with a flat board on the tip; the sharp end means a fight “at outrance,” with real weapons. Knowing the rules lets readers feel the stakes when a knight later makes that choice.
evidence: If he did so with the reverse of his lance
But if the shield was touched with the sharp end of the lance

questions.prompt: Reread the sentence that ends the laws. What is Scott’s verdict on John as a politician, and how has this chapter already proved it?
facilitatorNotes: John tries to buy popularity with games for the people but keeps throwing it away by “wanton aggression” on their feelings. The Rebecca jest a page earlier is an example, and Waldemar used the same word, “wantonness.” Students may add the purse-snatching of the last chapter.
evidence: which he was perpetually throwing down by some inconsiderate act of wanton aggression
It is the mere wantonness of insult

readings.title: Ivanhoe: The Challengers Hold the Field (Chapter VIII, part 2)
readings.challenge: Follow the narrator as he steps out of the story to comment and back in again, and ask what each comment does.
readings.focus: Glory and forgetting: the first jousts, a crowd’s taste for danger, and a Saxon’s wounded pride.
readings.context: Recap: Prince John’s followers talked him out of naming Rebecca Queen of Love and Beauty, and the heralds proclaimed the laws: five challengers, led by the Templar Brian de Bois-Guilbert, will meet all comers, and a shield struck with the sharp end of a lance means a fight with real weapons. The narrator pretends to follow an old “Saxon authority,” the Wardour Manuscript, which Scott made up. The “contemporary poet” is Samuel Taylor Coleridge; Scott quotes from memory the close of his “The Knight’s Tomb,” which this library also holds. Escutcheons are painted shields of arms; the five challengers are Bois-Guilbert, Malvoisin, Front-de-Bœuf, Grantmesnil and Ralph de Vipont, a Knight of St John (a Hospitaller, a member of a religious order of knights); the “attaint” is a fair, square strike; the melée (mêlée) is the general fight planned for the second day; clowns here are country people; “foiled” means beat back. The 1820 printing ends the paragraph about the unpopular challengers with a comma (“strangers and foreigners,”); the text keeps the page as printed.
readings.contentNote: Knights are thrown to the ground and disgraced. Cedric counts every Norman victory as a defeat for England; such national feeling is a perspective the novel examines.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the eighth chapter (printed “CHAPTER IX.”), from the opening of the barriers to the Prince’s talk of giving the prize to Bois-Guilbert; opens “At length the barriers were opened, and five knights, chosen by lot, advanced slowly into…”; closes “…Bois-Guilbert, who had, with a single spear, overthrown two knights, and foiled a third.”.

questions.prompt: Scott refuses to describe the knights’ arms and quotes three lines about knights who are “dust.” What is he saying about fame, and how does it change the way we watch the jousts that follow?
facilitatorNotes: Their castles are now “green mounds,” their names forgotten: the splendour is temporary. Then “Now, however, no whit anticipating the oblivion” turns back to knights fighting for a glory that will not last. Some readers find the passage melancholy; others hear irony about chivalry itself.
evidence: The knights are dust, And their good swords are rust
no whit anticipating the oblivion which awaited their names and feats

questions.prompt: Why are some spectators “rather disappointed” that the first knights choose the arms of courtesy? What comparison does the narrator make with his own day?
facilitatorNotes: They enjoy a tournament “exactly in proportion to the danger.” The same sort of people, he says, now applaud “the deepest tragedies”: a joke that links medieval bloodthirst to his readers’ own tastes. Students might ask whether audiences today are different.
evidence: were rather disappointed at the champions choosing the arms of courtesy
who, in the present day, applaud most highly the deepest tragedies

questions.prompt: Why is breaking a lance “athwart” an opponent counted more disgraceful than being thrown from the horse?
facilitatorNotes: A fall might be an accident; swerving shows clumsy handling of weapon and horse. The code values skill and control above luck.
evidence: a circumstance which was accounted more disgraceful than being actually unhorsed
whereas the other evinced awkwardness

questions.prompt: Wamba says it is better to be “the best man among a hundred, than the best man of two.” What does he mean, how do Athelstane and Cedric take it, and what does the exchange show about Cedric’s hopes?
facilitatorNotes: Athelstane will fight only in tomorrow’s crowded melée; Wamba mocks him with praise that sounds like a compliment. Athelstane hears a compliment, Cedric hears the joke and glares. Cedric wants Athelstane to save England’s honour, but his chosen champion is “too inert.” Some readers take Wamba to mean the melée is the safer stage; others that Athelstane avoids single combat.
evidence: It was better to be the best man among a hundred, than the best man of two.
Athelstane took the observation as a serious compliment
a disposition too inert and unambitious

readings.title: Ivanhoe: The Disinherited Knight (Chapter VIII, part 3)
readings.challenge: Judge a masked stranger only by what he does and says, without deciding who he is.
readings.focus: A challenge to the death, an exchange of boasts, and a raven on a shield.
readings.context: Recap: the five challengers, led by the Templar Bois-Guilbert, have beaten every knight who rode against them; Cedric fumes at the Norman triumph, the slow Athelstane will not fight, and Prince John is ready to give Bois-Guilbert the prize. Desdichado is Spanish for “disinherited”; Ralph de Vipont is the challenger from the Hospitallers; a pavilion is a large tent; the Templars were an order of fighting monks, sworn at first to poverty; “Gramercy” means many thanks; Gare le Corbeau is French for “Beware the raven”; hams are the backs of a horse’s thighs; a demi-volte is a half turn on horseback.
readings.contentNote: The Templar promises his challenger death before nightfall, and the two knights meet at full gallop.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the eighth chapter (printed “CHAPTER IX.”), from the solitary trumpet to the silence before the second course; opens “At length, as the Saracenic music of the challengers concluded one of those long and high…”; closes “…a silence, so deep and so dead, that it seemed the multitude were afraid even to breathe.”.

questions.prompt: What do the crowd’s shouts advise, and what does the stranger do instead? Why is everyone astonished?
facilitatorNotes: The crowd tells him to touch Vipont’s shield, “your cheapest bargain.” He rides to the strongest challenger and strikes Bois-Guilbert’s shield with the sharp end, a challenge to mortal combat. It suggests great confidence or a personal quarrel; the passage does not say which.
evidence: he has the least sure seat, he is your cheapest bargain
struck with the sharp end of his spear the shield of Brian de Bois-Guilbert until it rung again

questions.prompt: Compare the Templar’s words with the stranger’s replies. Who wins the exchange, and how?
facilitatorNotes: The Templar asks if he has confessed and promises he will “sleep in paradise.” The stranger answers that he is “fitter to meet death,” a jab at the Templar’s conscience, then repays mockery with mock courtesy: take a fresh horse and lance. Cool replies turn the threat back on the boaster.
evidence: I am fitter to meet death than thou art
for this night thou shalt sleep in paradise
I advise thee to take a fresh horse and a new lance

questions.prompt: Bois-Guilbert changes his shield. What did the old device mean, what does the new one say, and what does the narrator think of the Templars?
facilitatorNotes: Two knights sharing one horse recalled the order’s humble, poor beginnings, which the narrator says they traded for “arrogance and wealth.” The raven gripping a skull, with “Beware the raven,” is pure threat. The change of shields is a small picture of the order’s change.
evidence: representing two knights riding upon one horse
which they had since exchanged for the arrogance and wealth
Gare le Corbeau

questions.prompt: How does Scott make the first course feel fast and the pause after it feel slow? Point to words that set each pace.
facilitatorNotes: “The speed of lightning,” “the shock of a thunderbolt” and lances that “burst into shivers” give speed; then applause is hushed into a silence “so deep and so dead” that the crowd seem afraid to breathe. Readers wait with the crowd.
evidence: closed in the centre of the lists with the shock of a thunderbolt
hushed into a silence, so deep and so dead

readings.title: Ivanhoe: Five Victories (Chapter VIII, part 4)
readings.challenge: Compare how the stranger beats each challenger, and decide which victory tells most about him.
readings.focus: Skill, courtesy, and a toast that takes sides.
readings.context: Recap: an unknown knight calling himself Desdichado, the Disinherited, struck the Templar Bois-Guilbert’s shield with the sharp end of his lance; their first course ended even, and the crowd is silent before the second. A truncheon is a short staff of command; the girths are the straps that hold a saddle on; the beaver is the lower face-guard of a helmet; Cave, Adsum is Latin for “Beware, I am here”; a casque is a helmet.
readings.contentNote: Knights are thrown violently; one is carried off senseless and bleeding.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the eighth chapter (printed “CHAPTER IX.”), from the second course to the end of the chapter; opens “A few minutes pause having been allowed, that the combatants and their horses might…”; closes “…of the Prince and Marshals, announcing that day's honours to the Disinherited Knight.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the Templar fall? Does the narrator let us think the stranger simply outfought him?
facilitatorNotes: The stranger switched his aim to the helmet, “a mark more difficult to hit”; the Templar’s own blow was fair and strong, and he might have kept his seat “had not the girths of his saddle burst.” Scott gives the stranger the bolder skill but saves the Templar’s reputation; readers may say luck decided it, or that the harder aim earned the win.
evidence: changing his aim almost in the moment of encounter, he addressed it to the helmet
had not the girths of his saddle burst, he might not have been unhorsed

questions.prompt: What do the two knights say after the marshals part them, and what do their words promise for the rest of the story?
facilitatorNotes: The Templar hopes to meet “where there are none to separate us”; the stranger is ready on foot or horseback, with any weapon. Both promise a later fight without rules.
evidence: where there are none to separate us
On foot or horseback, with spear, with axe, or with sword

questions.prompt: The victor drinks “To all true English hearts, and to the confusion of foreign tyrants.” Who in the galleries would cheer, and who would take offence?
facilitatorNotes: Saxons such as Cedric, and the common people, hear a champion of England; the Norman challengers and Prince John, who favours them, hear an insult. Some readers think “foreign tyrants” points at John himself; the toast is also a clue to the stranger’s loyalties.
evidence: To all true English hearts, and to the confusion of foreign tyrants.

questions.prompt: Which of the four later victories shows something besides strength? Why might Scott include it?
facilitatorNotes: Against Grantmesnil, whose young horse reared, the stranger raised his lance and offered a second course; Grantmesnil yielded, beaten as much by courtesy as by skill. Courtesy is a knightly virtue too, set against the Templar’s threats and Vipont’s bloody fall.
evidence: the Disinherited Knight shewed as much courtesy as he had hitherto evinced courage and dexterity
avowing himself vanquished as much by the courtesy as by the address of his opponent

readings.title: Ivanhoe: Could It Be the King? (Chapter IX, part 1)
readings.challenge: Notice how guesses about a hidden face reveal more about the guessers than about the knight.
readings.focus: A prince’s fear of his absent brother.
readings.context: Recap: at the Ashby tournament an unknown knight, the Disinherited, has overthrown all five challengers, beginning with the Templar Bois-Guilbert, and drunk to “all true English hearts” and the confusion of “foreign tyrants.” This chapter is headed “CHAPTER X.” in the first edition, which gives the next chapter that number too; later editions call it Chapter IX. The motto describes the queen of an old English poem, “The Flower and the Leaf”; Agnus castus is a shrub. Incognito means with one’s name hidden; “atchieved” is an old spelling of achieved; “Wot ye” means do you know; the four seas “girth” (encircle) Britain; a Knight of St John is a Hospitaller, like the beaten Vipont, while Bracy sides with the rival Templars; “pitch” is height; “Over God’s forbode!” means God forbid. King Richard, John’s elder brother, has been a prisoner abroad on his way home from the Crusade, and John hopes to keep his throne.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the ninth chapter (printed “CHAPTER X.”), from its motto to the delivery of the war-horse; opens “—————— In the midst was seen A lady of a more majestic mien, By stature and by beauty…”; closes “…an answer might be returned in the deep and awful accents of Richard the Lion-hearted.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the marshals accept the knight’s refusal to show his face, while Prince John does not?
facilitatorNotes: Vows to stay incognito were common, so the marshals “pressed no farther.” John, already displeased that his favourites lost, sneers that the knight is disinherited “of his courtesy as of his lands.” His irritation turns a custom into an insult.
evidence: there was none more common than those by which they engaged to remain incognito
this same knight hath been disinherited, as well of his courtesy as of his lands

questions.prompt: Follow the guesses from Bracy, Fitzurse and the whisper in the train. Why does the last guess frighten John so much?
facilitatorNotes: Bracy cannot guess, Fitzurse suggests a crusader coming home, and someone whispers Richard himself. John turns “as pale as death” because his brother’s return would end his scheming, and he begs his followers to keep their promises. The fear shows how insecure his power is.
evidence: It might be the King—it might be Richard Cœur-de-Lion himself.
remember your promises and stand truly by me

questions.prompt: How does Fitzurse calm the Prince, and why is John not fully reassured?
facilitatorNotes: He argues from size: the knight lacks three inches of Richard’s height, and his horse could not carry Richard. John still trembles lest Richard’s “deep and awful accents” answer from the visor; a guilty conscience imagines the worst.
evidence: he wants three inches of King Richard's height
he trembled lest from the barred visor of the mailed form before him

questions.prompt: How does the Knight of St John answer Bracy’s boast? What does the quarrel show about John’s supporters?
facilitatorNotes: When Bracy praises the blow that unhorsed the Hospitaller Vipont, the Knight of St John retorts that “your Temple champion” rolled over three times. The two religious orders compete even in defeat; John’s side is split by small jealousies, and John has to silence them.
evidence: your Temple champion had no better luck
I saw Bois-Guilbert roll thrice over

readings.title: Ivanhoe: The Choice of a Queen (Chapter IX, part 2)
readings.challenge: Separate what Prince John says from why he says it, using the narrator’s list of his motives.
readings.focus: A prize, a hint, and a slow ride past the galleries.
readings.context: Recap: the marshals brought the masked victor before Prince John, who feared for a moment that the knight was his brother King Richard come home; John handed him the prize, a war-horse. Earlier that day John had proposed Rebecca, the daughter of Isaac of York, as Queen of Love and Beauty to insult the Saxons, and his followers stopped him. War-furniture is a horse’s armour and harness; the pummel (pommel) is the front of the saddle; a ducal crown is a duke’s coronet; licentious means immoral in his pleasures; predilection is preference; muscadine is a sweet wine.
readings.contentNote: The narrator recalls John’s “indecent” jest about Rebecca and calls him “licentious”; the ladies are inspected for their beauty, and Scott jokes about the older ones.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the ninth chapter (printed “CHAPTER X.”), from the knight’s silent bow to the Saxons’ gallery; opens “But the Disinherited Knight spoke not a word in reply to the compliment of the Prince,…”; closes “…for a huge goblet of muscadine, he quaffed it to the health of the Disinherited Knight.”.

questions.prompt: The knight answers John’s compliment with only a bow, then rides twice round the lists. Why does the narrator say this display was not vanity?
facilitatorNotes: He is showing the Prince’s gift “to the best advantage,” a courteous way of honouring it. His silence also keeps his identity hidden and leaves John uneasy. Some readers may still see pride in it.
evidence: spoke not a word in reply to the compliment of the Prince
was removed by the propriety shewn in exhibiting to the best advantage the princely reward

questions.prompt: Scott lists John’s motives for hinting that the knight should choose Alicia. Name three, and say which is the most cunning.
facilitatorNotes: To make people forget his jest about Rebecca, to please Waldemar, to win Alicia’s favour, and to make Waldemar the knight’s enemy if he chooses someone else. The last is a trap that works either way. Students may argue for another.
evidence: He wished to banish from the minds of the chivalry around him his own indecent and unacceptable jest
a powerful enemy in the person of Waldemar Fitzurse

questions.prompt: How do the ladies behave as the knight inspects the galleries, and what is the narrator’s tone?
facilitatorNotes: Some blush, some look proud or unconcerned, two or three laugh; the veiled ones are teased as “beauties of ten years standing.” The tone is gently mocking, a comedy of vanity in the middle of the pageant; some readers will find the joke about older women unkind.
evidence: Some blushed, some assumed an air of pride and dignity
these were beauties of ten years standing

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator say the Saxons’ gallery deserved the knight’s preference? Contrast Cedric, Rowena and Athelstane.
facilitatorNotes: Cedric leaned out over the balcony, cheering with “his whole heart and soul”; Rowena watched as closely but hid her feelings; even sluggish Athelstane drank the knight’s health. Rowena’s restraint hints at feelings she keeps private.
evidence: with half his body stretched over the balcony
though without betraying the same intense interest
Even the unmoved Athelstane had shewn symptoms of shaking off his apathy

readings.title: Ivanhoe: The Queen of Love and Beauty (Chapter IX, part 3)
readings.challenge: Watch how each speaker uses language itself, Saxon, French or silence, as a move in a contest.
readings.focus: A crown laid at a Saxon lady’s feet, a refused invitation, and a threat to an archer.
readings.context: Recap: at the tournament of Ashby an unknown knight, the Disinherited, has defeated all five challengers and must now name the Queen of Love and Beauty. Prince John hinted that he should choose Alicia, the daughter of John’s adviser Waldemar Fitzurse; the knight rode slowly past the galleries and stopped beneath the Lady Rowena, Cedric’s ward, whose Saxon party had cheered him all day. Before this passage Scott turns for five paragraphs to Isaac of York and his daughter Rebecca, watching the jousts; Isaac’s anxious remarks reveal that the knight’s horse and armour came from him. This chapter is headed “CHAPTER X.” in the first edition, which gives the next chapter that number too; later editions call it Chapter IX. Alfred the Great was the most famous Saxon king; a donative is a gift of money; a jennet is a small horse; outrecuidance (from French) is arrogance; Needwood and Charnwood are forests of the Midlands; the yeoman is the archer who answered John boldly earlier in the day.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, the ninth chapter (printed “CHAPTER X.”), from the champion’s pause beneath Rowena’s balcony to the end of the chapter; opens “Whether from indecision or some other motive of hesitation, the champion of the day…”; closes “…from two hours to two hours, surrounded the lists, and kept watch during the night.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the choice of Rowena a political act as well as a personal one? Use the two crowds’ reactions.
facilitatorNotes: Norman ladies murmur at the preference given to “a Saxon beauty,” while the people cheer “the Saxon Princess” and “the race of the immortal Alfred.” Crowning a Saxon at a Norman prince’s tournament answers John’s hint and his earlier insults to the Saxons; whether the knight meant it so is left open.
evidence: as much unused to see the preference given to a Saxon beauty
long live the race of the immortal Alfred!

questions.prompt: John’s remark about the knight’s eyes is meant to flatter Alicia. Why does it offend her father instead?
facilitatorNotes: Saying the knight’s eyes are “none of the clearest” announces to everyone that Alicia was passed over. Waldemar answers with dignity that every knight chooses freely and his daughter seeks no one’s favour. The narrator calls it John’s lifelong misfortune not to understand the people he wants to win.
evidence: his choice hath no less proved that his eyes are none of the clearest
My daughter courts distinction from no one

questions.prompt: Cedric answers for Rowena “in his native Saxon,” and John pretends not to understand. What is each of them doing with language?
facilitatorNotes: Cedric refuses the Norman banquet because they speak only “the language … of our fathers”: a proud rejection of Norman manners in the Saxon tongue. John is “well skilled” in Saxon but pretends ignorance, an insult in return, and mocks Rowena as a “mute sovereign.” Language becomes a weapon in the Saxon–Norman feud.
evidence: speak only the language, and practise only the manners of our fathers
